newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ASIAN EXOTICS - Regionals sag as dollar roars ahead.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN EXOTICS - Regionals sag as dollar roars ahead.

text.p: The U.S. dollar's relentless climb to a 47-month high of 122 yen in Asian trade dominated activity in most regional currency markets on Wednesday.
The dollar was quoted at 121.83/88 yen in Tokyo at 0445 GMT after rising above 122 yen earlier.

Only the typically stoic Singapore dollar stood its ground against the U.S. unit, boosted by a newspaper report quoting the city-state's finance minister saying he expected the currency to appreciate this year.
In an interview published by the Financial Times in its Wednesday edition, Richard Hu was quoted as saying some strengthening of the Sing dollar would be desirable to keep inflation down.
Dealers said market participants reacted to the report by unwinding long Malaysian ringgit/Sing dollar positions.
But they said active buying of the U.S. dollar around the S$1.4060 level by local banks sparked speculation of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, causing players to back off.
The de facto central bank typically intervenes in forex markets through local banks.
"Some people suspect that our authorities might be down there picking up (the U.S. dollar) because they can't have the Sing that strong either," said a senior dealer at an Asian bank.
Dealers said the U.S. dollar was likely to remain above S$1.4060 for the day but would have trouble rising above a large number of sell orders around S$1.4100.
"I don't think the article will have an impact over the medium term...the trend of the ringgit/Sing is still higher," said a Japanese bank dealer.
He said the cross was likely to stay supported around 0.5620 and face resistance at 0.5660 for the day.
In Indonesia, the rupiah was also relatively firm as players remained concerned about a possible liquidity squeeze.
Some Jakarta dealers said the early liquidity concern was exaggerated.
"I don't think liquidity is tight. It's merely that people are rushing to square overnight swap positions which triggered overnight money to increase," one dealer said.
A local bank dealer said offshore operators were seen entering the local market late on Tuesday, buying up tom/next swaps to a high 0.65/0.70 points.
"But local operators could not square the entire exposure, while some were speculating for a lower rate on Wednesday as overnight money fell to 10.0 percent late on Tuesday," he said.
"As everybody moves to cover his short position early this morning, rates are being driven up. I think short-term rates will decline later because there is sufficient supply at present," he added.

Dealers said overall sentiment on the rupiah remained firm as operators focused on a possible tightening in the money market on month-end factors, the lunar new year and the Eid al-Fitr celebrations in early February.
The local bank dealer said a temporary slowdown in the central bank's rupiah depreciation policy and weekly swap costs of some 3.5 points caused operators to go short in dollars.
The Thai baht slid against the dollar as the U.S. unit's surge forced the Bank of Thailand to fix the baht/dollar mid-rate at a 6-1/2-year low of 25.86. It was at 25.81 on Tuesday.
The baht was quoted at 25.890-25.895 to the dollar at 0445 GMT against 25.845-25.865 late on Tuesday.
Dealers said dollar/baht forward positions were being bought up, partly on concern about some Thai economic data due to be released on Thursday.

"With all the buying of dollars, the market needs to unwind its outright positions now. People took these positions early and failed to hedge them. They're now feeling the pinch because what they gain on interest may not cover the loss in terms of the exchange rate," said the Asian bank dealer in Singapore.
In Malaysia, the ringgit came under pressure from the rising dollar/majors and from players unwinding their ringgit/Sing positions.
But dealers said it was unlikely to weaken beyond 2.50 to the U.S. dollar for the day as market sentiment still favoured the Malaysian currency.

"I don't see dollar/ringgit going much higher even with the strong dollar/majors...Of all the regional currencies, Malaysia has got the best fundamentals at the moment," said the Singapore-based dealer.
-- Mantik Kusjanto in Jakarta (62-21-384-6364), Anuchit Nguyen in Bangkok (662) 652-0642 and Sonali Desai in Singapore (65-8703090)
